record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: If quasar redshifts measure cosmological distance, why should quasars evolve so that their average apparent brightness remains comparable across very different redshifts, while their number density peaks near redshift 2.5 to 3 and then declines at both lower and higher redshifts, instead of increasing naturally toward the earliest epochs as expected for galaxy seeds?

evidence.quote: Why QSOs should evolve in just this way to produce this coincidence of apparent magnitudes whatever it is its redshift?[127].

The standard model predicts that QSOs, the seeds of all galaxies, should be more numerous at earliest epochs, so apparently there is a problem here, which might be solved ad hoc, but not as a natural prediction of the model.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Under the standard cosmological model, quasars (QSOs) are assumed to be active galactic nuclei at cosmological distances, with their redshifts $z$ being a faithful measure of cosmological distance, and are commonly interpreted as seeds of galaxies that should therefore become more numerous toward the earliest cosmic epochs. Observations show two striking features of the QSO population:

(a) The mean apparent magnitude of quasars remains roughly comparable across a very wide range of redshifts, so that bright quasars are found at essentially all observed $z$, rather than systematically dimming with distance as a non-evolving population would.

(b) The comoving number density $n(z)$ of quasars rises with $z$, attains a maximum near $z \approx 2.5\!-\!3$, and then decreases at both lower redshifts and at higher redshifts, instead of monotonically increasing toward $z \to \infty$.

Provide, within the standard cosmological framework (with quasar redshifts cosmological in origin), a quantitative astrophysical model of quasar formation, fueling, and luminosity evolution that simultaneously and naturally predicts both phenomena (a) and (b)—i.e., that explains, without ad hoc tuning, why the luminosity evolution of quasars conspires with the distance–redshift relation to keep their typical apparent brightness nearly constant in $z$, while their comoving abundance peaks near $z \approx 2.5\!-\!3$ and declines on both sides of that peak.
artifact.status_search_result: The observed peak of quasar comoving number density near z ≈ 2–3 and its decline on both sides is well established, and modern models invoke luminosity-dependent density evolution ("AGN downsizing"), coevolution of supermassive black holes with host galaxies, and feedback-regulated accretion to fit the quasar luminosity function from z ~ 0 to z ~ 7. These models reproduce the qualitative trends but rely on prescriptions for black-hole seeding, accretion duty cycles, and feedback that are not derived from first principles, so the question of a fully natural, parameter-free explanation remains only partially resolved.

status_evidence.title: Quasar UV luminosity function evolution up to z = 8
status_evidence.snippet: The overall LF shape remains remarkably similar from z = 4 to 7, while the amplitude decreases substantially toward higher redshifts, with a clear indication of an accelerating decline at z ≥ 6.
status_evidence.claim: The decline of the quasar luminosity function at high redshift is observationally established and modeled phenomenologically.

status_evidence.title: The Evolution of Quasars - P.S. Osmer
status_evidence.snippet: Quasars increase in number with increasing redshift until z ∼ 2.5, when quasar activity peaks, with surveys for higher redshift quasars showing a steep decline.
status_evidence.claim: The peak of quasar number density near z≈2.5 and decline at higher z is a well-known observational feature.

status_evidence.title: The z = 5 quasar luminosity function from SDSS Stripe 82
status_evidence.snippet: Low-luminosity quasars show peak number density at lower redshifts than do high-luminosity quasars (luminosity-dependent density evolution / downsizing).
status_evidence.claim: Standard explanations invoke luminosity-dependent density evolution and AGN downsizing, which are phenomenological rather than first-principles derivations.
